newsitem.title: USA: Clinton claims credit for cutting deficit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton claims credit for cutting deficit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday claimed election-year credit for new figures showing a further decline in the U.S. budget deficit, saying it was evidence his economic policies were working.

Taking a jab at Republican rival Bob Dole's appeal to Americans to "wake up" and reject Clinton on Election Day Nov. 5, the president told a rousing campaign rally in this St. Louis suburb: "I would say that these results prove that America is awake and moving in the right direction."

Republicans contended Clinton deserved no credit because they had to drag him into reducing government spending after they took control of Congress in 1994 Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici of New Mexico said the lower deficit "vindicates our willingness to stand up to Bill Clinton."
Analysts said both Democrats and Republicans had helped to reduce the deficit with various actions raising taxes and cutting spending over the last six years.

"I would pat both parties and both branches of government on the back for these numbers," said Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington and former head of the Congressional Budget Office.

Clinton staked claim to credit on his visit to the "Show Me" state, nicknamed for Missourians' reputation for demanding proof of any claims. He stood on the steps of city hall in front of a large chart showing the country's red-ink spending was $290 billion in 1992 when he was elected and had declined every year he has been in office.

Two teens joined him on stage to pull a string unveiling the deficit figure for the 1996 budget year that ends Oct. 31 was $107 billion, the lowest budget deficit in 15 years, since 1981, Republican Ronald Reagan's first year as president.
Clinton said he was the first 20th century president to see the deficit decline in all four years of his term and had more than fulfilled a 1992 pledge to cut the deficit in half.

If not for deficit-spending under Reagan and his Republican successor George Bush, he asserted, the budget would be in surplus. "We all know that our budget would be in surplus today if it weren't for the interest we pay on the debt rung up in the 12 years before I took office," he said.

Franklin Raines, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which compiles the figure, said the drop reflected both stronger-than-expected growth that raised tax revenue and efforts to control government spending.
"About half is from the increase in economic growth and about half is from holding down spending," he told reporters on the third stop on a three-day, seven-state campaign trip.
To the Republican argument that the spending reductions they pushed were responsible for the favourable news, Raines argued that Republican contribution had been limited.

"The spending reductions since the Republican majority has been in place have been relatively modest compared to the overall total," he said. "Although we have been able work with them in the last year on the mutually acceptable budget ... if we had been able to do (that) earlier these numbers could have been much better."

Budget analyst Stan Collender of the Burson-Marsteller public relations firm said "if you divide the credit between Clinton and Congress, I would say about 75 percent goes to Clinton and about 25 percent to Congress."
"Remember Clinton got Congress to pass in 1993 a deficit reduction plan, with no Republican votes," Collender said.
Reischauer said the credit should be shared by two presidents -- Clinton and Bush. Both men pushed through Congress deficit-reduction packages that included tax hikes.

Reischauer said more than one session of Congress deserved credit as well. He noted that the Democrat-majority Congress of 1993 stopped a "stimulus" package of spending measures proposed by Clinton, while the Republican-majority Congress that took office in 1995 held spending below previous levels.
